nodes.label: Cursor-Based Pagination
nodes.rationale: OFFSET-based pagination scans all skipped rows, getting slower on deeper pages. Cursor-based pagination has O(1) performance regardless of page depth.

nodes.label: UPSERT Operations
nodes.rationale: Using separate SELECT-then-INSERT/UPDATE creates race conditions. Use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT for atomic upserts.

nodes.label: Advisory Locks
nodes.rationale: Advisory locks provide application-level coordination without requiring database rows to lock, reducing overhead.

nodes.label: Deadlock Prevention
nodes.rationale: Deadlocks occur when transactions lock resources in different orders. Always acquire locks in a consistent order.

nodes.label: Short Transactions
nodes.rationale: Long-running transactions hold locks that block other queries. Keep transactions as short as possible to reduce lock contention.

nodes.label: SKIP LOCKED Queue Processing
nodes.rationale: When multiple workers process a queue, SKIP LOCKED allows workers to process different rows without waiting, increasing worker queue throughput.

nodes.label: EXPLAIN ANALYZE
nodes.rationale: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and shows actual timings, revealing the true performance bottlenecks like seq scans, bad joins, or poor selectivity.

nodes.label: pg_stat_statements Extension
nodes.rationale: pg_stat_statements tracks execution statistics for all queries, helping identify slow and frequent queries that are candidates for optimization.

nodes.label: VACUUM and ANALYZE
nodes.rationale: Outdated statistics cause the query planner to make poor decisions. VACUUM reclaims space, ANALYZE updates statistics.

nodes.label: Composite Indexes
nodes.rationale: When queries filter on multiple columns, a composite index is more efficient than separate single-column indexes. Column order matters (equality first).

nodes.label: Covering Indexes
nodes.rationale: Covering indexes include all columns needed by a query, enabling index-only scans that skip table heap lookups entirely.

nodes.label: Index Types
nodes.rationale: Different index types excel at different query patterns (e.g. B-tree for comparison, GIN for arrays/JSONB, GiST for geometric, BRIN for large time-series).

nodes.label: Indexes on WHERE and JOIN Columns
nodes.rationale: Queries filtering or joining on unindexed columns cause full table scans, which become exponentially slower as tables grow.

nodes.label: Partial Indexes
nodes.rationale: Partial indexes only include rows matching a WHERE condition, making them smaller and faster when queries consistently filter on the same condition.

nodes.label: Safely Adding Constraints
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL does not support ADD CONSTRAINT IF NOT EXISTS. Use a DO block to check for existence before adding constraints to prevent migration failures.

nodes.label: Appropriate Data Types
nodes.rationale: Using appropriate data types (e.g. bigint instead of int, text instead of varchar, timestamptz for time) reduces storage and prevents overflow or timezone bugs.

nodes.label: Index Foreign Key Columns
nodes.rationale: Postgres does not automatically index foreign key columns. Missing indexes cause slow JOINs and CASCADE operations.

nodes.label: Lowercase Identifiers
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL folds unquoted identifiers to lowercase. Quoted mixed-case identifiers require quotes forever and cause compatibility issues with ORMs and tools.

nodes.label: Table Partitioning
nodes.rationale: Partitioning splits large tables (>100M rows) into smaller pieces (e.g., by range of time), improving query performance and enabling instant drop of old partitions.

nodes.label: Primary Key Strategy
nodes.rationale: Use bigint identity for sequential IDs. Use UUIDv7 (time-ordered) instead of random UUIDv4 to prevent index fragmentation in distributed systems.

nodes.label: Principle of Least Privilege
nodes.rationale: Grant only the minimum permissions required. Never use superuser for application queries. Revoke public defaults from schemas and tables.

nodes.label: Row Level Security Basics
nodes.rationale: Enabling RLS and creating policies isolates tenant data at the database level, preventing accidental data leaks from application-level filter bypasses.
